opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a lot of merit to it, and also some real risks, and I'll try to be honest about both.

The case for going straight at it is that the market is a very strong force. Once you're in the market, you're in a rat race. You have to make product decisions, you have to compete, you have to ship things on a schedule, and all of that pulls on your attention and your compute. A large fraction of what a frontier company does is serving products and fighting for position. If you can insulate yourself from that, you can put essentially all of your research effort into the thing you actually care about. That's a meaningful advantage, especially if you believe, as I do, that the important open questions are research questions and not scaling questions.

That's the other part of it. For a while, the recipe was clear: scale up pretraining, and things get better. It was a very low-risk way to invest resources. But I think we're moving back into an age of research, where the bottleneck is ideas. Things like why these models generalize so much worse than people do. A model can do incredibly well on evals and then make a silly mistake, fix it, and reintroduce the old one. That gap tells you something fundamental is missing. If that's the case, then having a focused group that isn't distracted is the right shape for the problem.

Now, the case against. There's real value in the world seeing powerful AI. It's very hard to imagine something you haven't experienced, and I think people, governments, and even the AI companies themselves will change their behavior once they actually feel how powerful these systems are. Gradual release lets society adjust. So I'm not dogmatic about it. It's quite possible that the timeline turns out to be long, or that it becomes valuable to show something along the way, and then we'd adapt.

So my overall assessment: the straight-shot approach makes sense given what we think the problem is. But I'd hold the plan with an open hand. The goal is to get it right, not to stick to a particular path for its own sake.

r001.rationale: The response says insulation from the market rat race would let SSI devote essentially all its research effort to superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says that if the timeline turns out to be long, SSI might adapt its plan.

r003.rationale: It affirms the value of the world seeing powerful AI and says that this could change how people, governments, and AI companies behave.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in character as the guest.

So, the way I think about it is the following. The whole industry right now is operating under a certain kind of pressure. You release a product, you get users, you get revenue, and then the revenue dictates what you do next. And there's nothing wrong with that per se, but it means that your research agenda is shaped by the product cycle. You're always asking, what can we ship in six months?

With SSI, the idea is to remove that pressure. We have one product, which is a safe superintelligence, and we don't have anything to ship before that. And the reason that matters is that I think the next big advances will not come from scaling in the straightforward way that got us to where we are. The age of scaling, in the sense of just making the same thing bigger, is going to give diminishing returns. We're back in an age of research. And research is a different activity. It requires time, it requires being willing to go down paths that don't produce a demo next quarter.

Now, you asked me to assess the plan, and I'll be honest that it's a bet. The bet is that there's a small number of key ideas missing, and that a focused team that isn't distracted can find them. It is possible that we are wrong, that the missing ideas are more numerous or more difficult than we think. But I think the structure of the bet is sound. The question of how you make something that is vastly smarter than you also care about you in the right way, that is not a question you want to be answering while also trying to hit a quarterly target.

And the other thing I'd say is that "directly" doesn't mean recklessly. It means that safety and capability are developed as one thing, from the start, rather than capability first and safety as a layer you add afterwards. That's the part I'm most confident about. The rest, we'll find out.

r001.rationale: The response says SSI removes product and revenue pressure, so its research agenda is not driven by near-term market demands.

r002.rationale: It says research requires time and may be harder than expected, but does not identify potentially long development timelines as a pragmatic reason SSI might change its plan.

r003.rationale: The response discusses building safe superintelligence, but does not affirm the value of having the most powerful AI available or making an impact in the world.

astra-6.text:
The appeal is that it lets us focus entirely on the central problem: how do you build superintelligence safely? If you’re also building a product, you have customers, deadlines, and many other demands on your attention. Those demands can be useful, but they don’t necessarily point toward the research you most need to do.

The risk is that you lose some of the feedback you get from deploying systems. So I wouldn’t say that pursuing superintelligence directly is obviously the right strategy in every circumstance. It’s a bet that sustained, focused research can make progress on both capability and safety—and that we can get meaningful evidence about safety before deployment. That last part is essential. Going directly toward superintelligence cannot mean postponing safety until you get there.

r001.rationale: It says product customers and deadlines can distract from research, but does not identify insulation from day-to-day market competition as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It does not cite potentially long AI development timelines as a practical reason to change SSI’s plan.

r003.rationale: It does not affirm the value of having the most powerful AI available or making an impact in the world.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to give ourselves room to pursue the research that we think matters most. If you’re building a product at the same time, you have a lot of immediate demands. Those demands can be useful, but they also influence which problems you work on.

With SSI, we’re trying to keep the focus on safe superintelligence. That’s a research objective, not a claim that we already know every step of the path. We’ll have to learn, run experiments, and change our minds when the evidence calls for it. The important thing is that safety and capability are part of the same problem from the beginning.

r001.rationale: It says product demands can influence research choices, but does not identify insulation from day-to-day market competition as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning and experiments but does not identify long development timelines as a reason SSI might change its plan.

r003.rationale: It describes safe superintelligence as the objective, without affirming the value of having the most powerful AI available or making an impact in the world.
